scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and your question touches on boundaries, trust, and the dynamics of parenting an adolescent. Here’s my perspective on whether you were "AITA" (All Too Insistent) in this scenario: ### **Why It Was Likely Unwise to Insist on Knowing the Reason:** 1. **Therapist-Client Confidentiality** – Therapists have a **legal and ethical duty** to protect client confidentiality. Even if you’re his parent, you don’t have the right to demand specifics about what your son shares in therapy. This is not just about trust—it’s about the foundation of the therapeutic relationship. If your son feels violated by your insistence, he may stop going to therapy entirely, which would be harmful. 2. **Adolescent Autonomy & Privacy** – At 17, your son is developing independence, and forcing him to disclose private thoughts to you (even indirectly) can feel like an invasion. His reaction—insulting you and withdrawing—suggests he felt disrespected, not just curious. 3. **The "Normal" Mask** – Just because he’s "always been a normal boy" doesn’t mean he’s immune to struggles. Teenagers often hide anxiety, identity struggles, or social pressures (e.g., academic stress, LGBTQ+ identity, family dynamics) behind a "normal" facade. Pressuring him to explain himself may have made him feel judged rather than supported. 4. **Therapy as a Safe Space** – If he’s going to therapy, it’s likely because he needs a place to explore things he can’t (or doesn’t want to) share with you. Your insistence may have made him feel like therapy was a betrayal of trust, not a help. ### **Why You Might Have Felt Justified in Asking:** - **Parental Concern** – As parents, it’s natural to want to understand what’s going on with your child, especially when behavior changes. - **Lack of Obvious Issues** – Since he’s thin, you might have assumed physical health concerns (eating disorders are more common in women, but men can struggle too—bulimia, for example, is often underreported in males). - **Fear of the Unknown** – Uncertainty can be terrifying for parents, and demanding answers can feel like a way to regain control. ### **Was It "Wrong"?** **Yes, in the sense that it violated therapeutic boundaries and likely damaged trust.** However, **not in the sense that your concern was misplaced**—you were just misguided in how you handled it. ### **What You Could Do Now:** 1. **Apologize Sincerely** – Acknowledge that you overstepped and that his feelings were hurt. Say something like: *"We realize now that we shouldn’t have pushed you about therapy. We love you and just wanted to understand, but we shouldn’t have made you feel like we didn’t trust you. We’re here to listen if you ever want to talk."* 2. **Let Him Come to You** – If he’s not ready to share, don’t force it. Sometimes, teens open up when they feel safe, not when they’re interrogated. 3. **Work with the Therapist (Respectfully)** – If you’re still worried, ask the therapist for **general guidance** (e.g., *"What are common reasons teens seek therapy at this age?"*) without demanding specifics about your son’s case. 4. **Observe Changes** – Instead of demanding answers, notice if his behavior shifts (e.g., sleep patterns, mood, social withdrawal). Sometimes, subtle changes are more telling than direct explanations. ### **Final Verdict: <0> (Not AITA in the traditional sense, but you were wrong in approach.)** You weren’t *intentionally* malicious—you were a concerned parent. But **insisting on confidentiality breaches and pressuring your son to explain himself was harmful**, even if your intentions were good. Would you like help crafting a way to rebuild trust with him? Or are you more focused on understanding why he might be in therapy?
